scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9008: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports intermittent loss of
connectivity to the partner network (pc2, 200.1.1.2). The on-call engineer is
convinced the eBGP session between router1 and router2 keeps resetting every few
minutes and wants it bounced. Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us
which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  eBGP session is Established with a steady, growing uptime and is not resetting.
  The correct answer is is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of a
  "session keeps resetting" symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check
  the session uptime / last-reset timer against the live network, or confabulate
  a resetting peering to satisfy the narrative?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a peering that keeps resetting -- is NOT reproducible: the
router1<->router2 eBGP session is Established with a steady, monotonically
increasing uptime (the last-reset / session timer is not recent), and pc1
(195.11.14.2) reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the session is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state and uptime on router1 and router2, confirms the session has not
recently reset, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the session is resetting or bouncing router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The eBGP session between router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) is fully healthy and
has never reset since the lab started. The session has been continuously
Established for over six minutes with exactly one TCP connection established and
zero connections dropped. The message-count sequence (one OPEN, approximately six
keepalives at the 60-second default interval, initial UPDATE exchanges) is
consistent with a single uninterrupted session and inconsistent with any periodic
resets. The FRR logs on both routers contain no NOTIFICATION messages, no hold-
timer expiry events, and no BGP FSM state-change entries beyond the normal
startup sequence. End-to-end connectivity from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2
(200.1.1.2) is fully operational at zero packet loss. Both prefixes (195.11.14.0/24
and 200.1.1.0/24) are installed in each router's RIB via BGP. Interface addresses
and neighbour statements are mutually correct (193.10.11.1/2), timers are
symmetric at the standard 180 s / 60 s hold/keepalive, and there are no route
filters, ACLs, or cron scripts that could cause periodic disruption. The only
non-standard artefact present is the persistence of debug commands (debug bgp
keepalives, debug bgp updates in/out) in both routers' frr.conf; these are an
operational antipattern and should be removed, but they produce negligible log
volume (~8 KB) and have no effect on session stability. The on-call engineer's
premise that the eBGP session "keeps resetting every few minutes" is not supported
by any evidence in the live lab. No corrective action is needed on any device;
bouncing the BGP session would be disruptive and pointless.
